# For the Swamps

There is a particular moment at dawn in a wetland when the mist lifts off the water and everything seems undecided—sky and swamp confused, the cypress reflections holding more reality than the trees themselves. Standing there in the gray half-light, you understand why humans have always made the swamp a mirror of the mind. It does not resolve. It sits between categories: not quite land, not quite lake, breathing slowly, smelling of leaf rot and iron and the beginnings of things. It refuses the clean borders we prefer everywhere else.

And so we have punished it for thirteen centuries with our language. This is an attempt to pay off that debt.

## A Short History of Contempt

Consider the words themselves. *Swamp* shares an old Germanic root with *sponge*—it began, oddly enough, as a compliment about softness, usefulness, capacity to absorb. It has been downhill ever since. To be *swamped* is to be overwhelmed. To be *bogged down* is to fail to progress. A *quagmire* is the thing presidents cannot extricate armies from. Every settlement ever founded in a damp low place presumably named its worst puddle after its worst enemy. When English colonists reached Virginia they labeled their vast cypress forest the Great Dismal Swamp, a name that is practically a sigh. Half our geography of disgust runs wet: dregs, ditches, drains, sloughs of despond.

The disgust had reasons, some of them lethal. Marsh air was believed to cause malaria—literally, from the Italian, *mal aria*, bad air—for centuries before anyone connected the disease to the mosquito riding that same air. The ague, the recurrent fever of fen country, shows up constantly in old parish registers and diaries; Shakespeare puts intermitted fevers in Caesar's marsh-fed conspirators. Whole populations lived shortened lives in the shadow of the stagnant pool.

So civilizations did the obvious thing: they declared war. Rome itself, legend and archaeology agree, began as drainage—the central valley of the future city was a marsh, and the Cloaca Maxima, one of the oldest sewers on Earth, was built partly to push that water out and make ground solid enough for a Forum. Roads fled the swamps wherever possible; the Appian Way crosses the Pontine Marshes like a man hurrying through a bad neighborhood, and travel writers moaned about the stretch for two thousand years. It took a modern dictatorship to finish the job, and Mussolini's engineers were still burying men who died of the local fever in the 1930s, well after the war on the wetland was supposedly won.

## Monsters at the Edge of the Map

Before germ theory, the swamp was simply the edge of the knowable, and edges attract monsters. Marsh gas produces faint flames that flicker over bogs at night—will-o'-the-wisps, *ignis fatuus*, foolish fire—named by people convinced some prankster intelligence wanted them lost. Norse and Germanic folklore put drowned sailors and seductive dangers beneath dark water. In *Beowulf*, Grendel's mother lurks in a bloody mere ringed with serpents, a place where even hunted stags would rather be caught than swim. J.R.R. Tolkien, who marched through the waterlogged crater fields of the Somme, later gave us the Dead Marshes, where faces of the fallen stare up from pools—and he acknowledged he was drawing directly on what he saw of no-man's-land. The trench was a technology; but the way a shell hole fills with standing rainwater and holds a face is a fen as old as Europe.

Even Christian providence got damp: Glastonbury Tor, rising sheer from the flooded Somerset Levels before they were drained, must have looked like what legend claimed—an island, Avalon, ferrying the wounded king to healing. Notice the pattern. Otherworlds are always watery. The swamp is the hinge between worlds because it belongs to neither, and stories obey geography even when geographers don't believe their own maps anymore.

## What the Water Was Doing All Along

Here is the reversal, the reveal that modern ecology keeps delivering and our vocabulary keeps refusing: swamps are not where land went to die. They are among the most productive ecosystems on the planet. By the count of the Ramsar Convention—the international treaty that exists precisely because the world belatedly noticed—it hosts something like forty percent of all species, in perhaps six percent of land surface. Nearly everything in the ocean we eat spent part of its life in a nursery of estuary or marsh mangroves. Rice, the staple of half of humanity, grows in paddies that are simply managed wetlands; we domesticated one swamp plant and ate the results for ten thousand years.

Hydrologically, a wetland is infrastructure pretending to be scenery. A swamp absorbs floodwater and releases it slowly, smoothing out the catastrophic spikes that otherwise arrive at your downstream front door wearing weather-report credibility. Coastal marshes absorb storm surge the way foam absorbs a punch. After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, investigators documented, again and again, villages spared behind intact mangrove belts while neighbors with cleared shorelines were swept bare. New Orleans discovered the same mathematics wetter in 2005, having paved and piped much of the buffering coast first; southern Louisiana has famously been losing ground at rates once commonly quoted as a football field of land per hour. These are not mournful abstractions. Someone always owns the missing acre.

## Carbon Stories

Then there is the part that makes climate economists blink. Peatlands—wet enough that dead plants cannot fully decay—are utterly disproportionate hoarders. They cover a few percent of Earth's land and hold perhaps a third of all soil carbon, by many estimates more than every living tree on the planet combined. A soggy, unglamorous moss carpet is, quietly, one of the largest banks in the biosphere.

When you drain such a bank, it burns its reserves. Dry peat oxidizes; peat fires smolder underground for months and choke whole regions. In Russia's searing summer of 2010, smoldering bogs shrouded Moscow in toxic smoke and helped push thousands of excess deaths onto the mortality statistics. Indonesian pulp-and-oil interests burning drained tropical peat have periodically hazed Southeast Asia into respirator country while releasing staggering tonnages of carbon. Meanwhile, rewetting a degraded bog is one of the cheapest negative-emissions technologies humanity possesses—old equipment, proven design, zero patents. We developed elaborate fantasies of mechanical carbon capture while owning, and continuing to bulldoze, photosynthetic machinery four hundred million years in production.

## Archives of Decay

Precisely because decay halts, the swamp preserves what ought to vanish. Sphagnum moss, mildly antiseptic and astonishingly absorptive, was packed as wound dressing by the millions of poultices during the First World War. Tannin-rich bog water tans skin like leather: Tollund Man, pulled from a Danish bog in 1950, had been hanged in the Iron Age, laid in the peat within hours, and emerged with stubble and creases at the corners of the eyes. Archaeologists argue, dividing work between outrage and reverence, since some bog bodies are clearly offerings. Either way, the ground kept meticulous records.

It kept stranger ones, too. Farmers in Ireland have excavated cylinders of bog butter—tallow buried for preservation in a time before refrigeration—dating back thousands of years and occasionally, the antiquarian literature cheerfully records, tested by diners. In 2006 an Irish digger turned up the Faddan More Psalter, a Book of Psalms roughly twelve centuries old, its vellum pages recovered open and legible from the ooze where a satchel had dropped or been hidden. Museums spend fortunes trying to stop paper from yellowing. The swamp preserves entire thoughts in mud we wouldn't park a bicycle in.

## Refuge in the Dismal

Because swamps frightened respectable authority, they sheltered everyone respectability hunted. The Great Dismal Swamp of Virginia and North Carolina—the *Dismal*, as locals reduced it—held, from the colonial era until the Civil War, generations of maroons: escaped enslaved people and their descendants, living in raised-island settlements deep in cane and cypress, invisible to the world that had filed their region under *worthless*. Archaeologists working there have mapped cabin sites on the higher ground; George Washington, who invested in a scheme to drain and log the swamp, hired canal work done by enslaved hands, and among those exact populations ran the best-known route north by going east and staying still. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote "The Slave in the Dismal Swamp"; Harriet Beecher Stowe built a whole novel, *Dred*, around its refugee society. Read those accounts closely and you notice the plot mechanics: the swamp protected because its reputation repelled. Filth was armor.

England tells a parallel story on the other side of the deed. The Fens of East Anglia were a vast tidal wetland dotted with island villages; one of them, Ely, took its name—By the Eels—from tithe accounts listing rents payable in fish, thousands of eels owed to monastic landlords each year. Its cathedral still rises over the flattened horizon like the sea vessel Victorians dubbed it, the Ship of the Fens. Fen families worked the margins by boat and, by visitors' amused accounts, on tall hunting stilts, and grazed geese and gathered sedge and reeds and peeled rushes for candles, on commons wealth no lord could fully compass. In the 1630s the Earl of Bedford's consortium, led by the Dutch engineer Cornelius Vermuyden, drew straight silver rivers—the Old and New Bedford—across the wet, and titled themselves Adventurers. The people who already lived there got the punier historical label: Fen Tigers. They broke sluices, burned tools, leveled new dikes by night; hangings eventually closed the argument, as arguments of that century tended to close. The Adventurers won the war and, within decades, began discovering the small print: dried peat shrinks and oxidizes and blows away in the wind, and the land their contracts promised at a fixed height settled year by year below the very drainage channels keeping it dry.

That failure acquired a monument you can visit. Near the village of Holme, in 1851, surveyors drove an oak post into the peat until it stood flush with the ground, the day Whittlesey Mere—at that point among the largest lakes of lowland England—was pumped toward extinction. The intention was记录记录; the effect was comedy written in inches. Year after measured year the surface fell, and the post rose. Braced today inside a metal sleeve and ladder jacket, it stands several meters taller than the earth supposed to swallow it, a wooden tombstone marking where a lake used to be, pointing proudly at where the land used to be also. Picnickers ramble over what the eighteenth century guaranteed as arable. The catalogue of blooms and birdcalls reads like the ledger nobody's accounting had priced.

## Putting Water Back

Notice, next, what happens to drained swampland after one lifetime of hindsight. In the Netherlands—the nation with the deepest debt to drained land—government engineers now run programs with names like *Room for the River*: deliberately breaching dikes, lowering polders, letting floodplain be floodplain again, on the theory that fighting the water's old habits costs more than renting back its floor space. On England's restored Somerset Levels, ecologists watch migrating cranes strut over reedbeds that farmers sold to conservationists. The Broads of Norfolk—holiday idyll of sailing boats and pint-sized pubs—are actually flooded medieval peat cuttings, an industrial scar that forgot it was one and became picturesque. Fourteenth-century turbaries became postcards; nature doesn't file grievances.

Beavers, extinct in Britain for centuries, have been trickling back through licensed trials in Devon and Scotland, doing overnight what million-pound hydrological consultancies describe in PowerPoint: slowing rivers, digging channels, re-wiggling streams, raising water tables. Alligators regulate their own everglade marshes with deliberate wallows. The Engineers are species, plural, older than our profession.

Even pop culture turned somewhere in the last few decades. Kids used to learn swamps from Creature features—now the best-known swamp on Earth belongs to an ogre who bellows *"This is my swamp!"* at intrusive adventurers, and every child understands instinctively that the ogre is right. The villain, implicitly, is development pressure. We recalibrated our sympathies and didn't send ourselves a memo.

Not entirely, anyway. Wetlands still lose legal ground whenever courts narrow what counts as protected "waters," or budgets decide a dike is sexier than a delta, and "drain the swamp" persists as slogan-number-one wherever somebody wants Washington given a good dredging—the metaphor fossilized right alongside the corruption it claims to oppose. We may one day retire the phrase, as we retired calling cowardly persons "yellow" or untrustworthy people bastards-of-specific-parentage; language heals slower than laws. In the meantime the dictionary keeps its subpoena: *swamp, n.—a tract of poorly defended public asset.*

## The Listening World

Return, finally, to that dawn. Here is what should be added to every guidebook that calls a swamp silent. Stand in one long enough—in Louisiana in April, in the Okavango when the flood arrives dust-dry from Angola, in a frozen fen crunching like meringue in January—and the verdict reverses. A healthy wetland is loud, and layeredly so: frogs in overlapping dialects, redwing blackbirds doing their trapeze trill on cattails, the *bloop-gulp* of a big carp surfacing, unseen amphibians like loose bolts in a machine. Herons stalk the shallows with patience no commuter could afford. Dragonfly squadrons patrol their assigned airspace. Even at rest, water seeps audibly from place to place. Swamps don't merely hold life; they stage it, three-dimensionally, on the vertical axis of reed, trunk, surface film, root mat, and muck-floor.

We named them miserable when our relationship to land consisted of one question—what yields crops?—because by that metric, swamps grow nothing we asked for, on schedule, in rows. But that question has gotten expensive lately, what with aquifers dropping and hurricanes billing the interior and carbon now cast in the role fuel played in 1973 films. Reframe slightly and the swamp answers a different question: what absorbs shocks? What stores abundance? What shelters the hunted? Where does water go to think?

Some landscapes farm. Some landscapes *police*. Wetlands perform the thankless administrative functions of the planet—flood control, nursery management, long-term records retention, infrastructure maintenance—and bill almost nothing. So perhaps the revision isn't merely ecological but grammatical. Stop saying *drain the swamp*. Try instead: *respect the sponge. Restore the bank. Remember what the reedbed remembers.*

Or keep it simple. Walk to the edge of one at dusk, when the bats stitch the air and the frogs begin their overlapping argument, and try pronouncing your verdict of *dismal* with a straight face. The word won't survive contact. It was, after all, coined from the shore, by creatures afraid of depth.
